units.translation: After the voting has been completed, Athena rises once more to give one final rule; from her speech the manner of the voting that has taken place also becomes clear, as not entirely identical with the later one described by ⟦1⟧. Two urns were also in use later, but a bronze one for the valid ⟦2⟧, and a wooden one for the invalid; the juror, however, received two ⟦3⟧, one ⟦4⟧ for acquittal and one ⟦5⟧ for condemnation, and threw one into each urn, while completely preserving the secrecy of the vote. Here, by contrast, as also in the ⟦6⟧, each voter has only one ⟦7⟧, and throws it into the one or the other vessel (⟦8⟧ ⟦9⟧, ⟦10⟧), according as he condemns or acquits. In order for this vote to be secret, the vessels had to stand in a concealed place. That this manner of voting continued through the 5th century is evident from Aristoph. ⟦11⟧. 987 f. and from Phrynichos ⟦12⟧ in Harp. ⟦13⟧: ⟦14⟧. ⟦15⟧, ⟦16⟧. That Athena likewise would have voted now was G. Hermann's opinion, which was contested by Müller and especially by Schömann; it is hardly shared by anyone any longer. That the vote that took place was secret emerges clearly from what follows; how then can Athena take part in this vote and vote publicly? She also does not say ⟦17⟧, but ⟦18⟧, namely for the case of an equality of votes in the urns, and there it is surely clear that the whole expression is figurative and not literal, and only the principle that was also valid later in Athens is being set up (⟦19⟧): ⟦20⟧, ⟦21⟧ (⟦22⟧). Thus ⟦23⟧ and everything else stands figuratively in the passage of the Agamemnon, and in many places of the Suppliants (640. 645. 739 etc.) ⟦24⟧ and the like of the decision of the Argives made by show of hands;
This voting-urn of yours is the one that acquits
